name: Długi Targ & Neptune Fountain
desc: The Hanseatic main square: Neptune's bronze fountain (1633), Artus Court, the Green Gate and a wall of stepped gables.
why: This is the postcard and the natural meeting point. Everything in the Old Town is within 400 m of it.
tip: Meet at Neptune, not at 'the old town' — the square has four exits and you will lose someone.

name: Artus Court (Dwór Artusa)
hours: Mon 10–16 (free) · Tue closed · Wed–Sun 10–16, Thu to 18
desc: The guildhall of Gdańsk's merchant brotherhoods: a 12-metre tiled stove, ship models, and paintings of kings and sea battles.
why: It explains how a trading city governed itself — and the interior is genuinely spectacular for 35 zł.
tip: Free on Monday 26 Oct with the Muzeum Gdańska free-day; do it together with the Town Hall next door.

name: Green Gate (Brama Zielona)
desc: A 1568 gate built as a royal residence, now a gallery, framing the view from Długi Targ down to the Motława.
why: Best photo angle in the city: stand at Neptune and shoot through the gate arches to the river.
tip: The archway is the shortcut from the square to Długie Pobrzeże — use it instead of walking around.

name: St Mary's Basilica
desc: The largest brick church in the world — 30,000 people fit inside, 400 steps to the tower, and a 15th-century astronomical clock.
why: The tower gives the only rooftop panorama of the Old Town, and the clock performs at 11:57 daily for free.
tip: Tower closes in strong wind — Sunday's 62 km/h gusts will shut it. Climb Saturday or Monday instead.

name: ul. Mariacka
desc: A cobbled canyon of stone stoops, gargoyles and amber workshops running from St Mary's to the river.
why: The most atmospheric 200 metres in Gdańsk, and where you buy amber without the pier pressure.
tip: Buy amber here, not on Długi Targ: same stones, 20–30% cheaper, and you can watch them work.

name: The Crane (Żuraw)
desc: Europe's largest surviving medieval port crane, with two wooden tread-wheels men once walked inside to lift cargo.
why: The mechanism is intact and you can stand inside it — plus the riverside outside is the best free view in the city.
tip: The outside is free and better at dusk. Pay only if you like machinery; the exhibition is small.

name: SS Sołdek
desc: A 1949 coal-fired steamship — the first ship built entirely in post-war Gdańsk — with engine room, hold and bridge open.
why: You climb into a real steam engine room. Small, cheap, and genuinely interesting even if you are not a ship person.
tip: Combine with the Ołowianka walk and the Philharmonic; all three are within 200 m.

name: Maritime Culture Centre
desc: The hands-on branch of the Maritime Museum: ship simulators, a kids' harbour, and how a port actually works.
why: If the weather kills the harbour, this is the next best thing — and it is warm.
tip: Good rainy-day filler with the Sołdek next door; both on one ticket if you ask.

name: Museum of the Second World War
desc: Poland's most visited museum: a vast underground exhibition on 1939–45, occupation, the Holocaust and resistance.
why: The floor shakes with bomber engines and the building leans over you. Few museums in Europe hit this hard.
tip: Book a timed slot the night before; Sunday is NOT free (Tuesday is). Last 30 min = 17 zł tickets.

name: European Solidarity Centre
desc: The Solidarity story inside the rust-coloured shipyard building: the 1980 strikes, Wałęsa, martial law, 1989.
why: You walk through the gate where the movement started, and the rooftop terrace over the cranes is free.
tip: Rooftop and lobby cost nothing — go up even if you skip the exhibition.

name: Museum of Amber
desc: The largest amber collection in Poland, inside a 14th-century mill: inclusions, sun stones, and the amber trade that built Gdańsk.
why: Free on Monday 26 Oct — the single best cultural deal of your dates.
tip: Arrive before 11:00 to dodge school groups; the basement floor is the best part.

name: Main Town Hall
hours: Mon 10–16 (free) · Tue closed · Wed–Sun 10–16, Thu to 18
desc: Renaissance town hall with the gilded Red Hall, carillon and a tower looking straight down Długa to the river.
why: Free on Monday, and the tower view is the classic Gdańsk photograph from above.
tip: No lift — 200+ steps. Wind can close the tower; the Red Hall alone is worth the stop.

name: Uphagen House
desc: A restored 18th-century merchant's house on Długa with period furniture, tiled stoves and a rococo staircase.
why: Shows how the people who built this city actually lived — three minutes from the crowds, usually empty.
tip: Skip if you are museum-ed out; do it if you liked the Amber Museum and want more interiors.

name: National Museum — Old Art
desc: Housed in a former Franciscan monastery: Dutch and Flemish painting, Gdańsk silver, furniture and the famous Last Judgement triptych.
why: The cheapest serious art museum in the city (15 zł) and almost always quiet.
tip: Tuesday is free for all branches — but you are leaving Monday, so pay the 15 zł on Sunday.

name: Abbots' Palace (Pałac Opatów)
desc: A rococo palace in Oliwa Park holding the National Museum's modern art and ceramics, with a garden café.
why: Pairs perfectly with the Oliwa organ — 5 minutes' walk, and the park outside is free.
tip: Closed Mondays, so if Monday is your Oliwa day, do the cathedral and park instead.

name: Hevelianum & Góra Gradowa
desc: A 19th-century Prussian fort on a hill 10 minutes from the Old Town, now a science centre with a 360° panorama.
why: The best free sunset viewpoint in central Gdańsk and almost no tourists.
tip: Take beers up for the 17:27 sunset — locals do, and it is legal.

name: Westerplatte
desc: Where the war in Europe began at 04:48 on 1 September 1939: ruined barracks, the Defenders' Monument, and a windswept peninsula between harbour and sea.
why: The boat ride there passes the shipyards, cranes and container terminal — half the attraction is the journey.
tip: Only on a dry, low-wind day. Sunday's gale would be miserable; Monday gusts 46 are borderline.

name: Wisłoujście Fortress
hours: Seasonal — usually closed late Oct, check
desc: A 17th-century fortress guarding the harbour mouth, with a circular brick tower and star-shaped earthworks.
why: Atmospheric and almost empty — but only if it is open, and in late October it often is not.
tip: Ring ahead. If closed, skip: the drive there is pure industrial estate.

name: Nowy Port Lighthouse
desc: An 1894 lighthouse with a time ball, looking across the harbour mouth to Westerplatte and the open Baltic.
why: Industrial, off-grid, and the best view of the port. Pairs with Westerplatte by car.
tip: Check opening before travelling — hours shrink sharply in late October.

name: Oliwa Cathedral
desc: A vast Cistercian cathedral with a famous 18th-century organ — 7,896 pipes, moving angels and trumpeting figures.
why: A 20-minute mechanical theatre, not a church service. The best value cultural experience in Gdańsk.
tip: Monday: demos at 11:00 and 12:00. Be there 10:45 and sit centre-front.

name: St Catherine's Church & carillon
desc: Gdańsk's oldest parish church, with a 50-bell carillon that plays from the tower and a small clock museum inside.
why: The carillon recital is a five-minute free concert that most visitors walk straight past.
tip: Ask at the door for the next carillon time — usually on the hour in the afternoon.

name: St Nicholas' Church
desc: A dark, soaring Dominican church with a star-vaulted nave and one of the best baroque altars in Pomerania.
why: Quiet, free, and 90 seconds from Długi Targ — a good five-minute escape from the crowd.
tip: Look up: the vault and the pulpit are the reason to come in.

name: Shakespeare Theatre (Teatr Szekspirowski)
desc: A modern theatre with a retractable roof over an Elizabethan-style courtyard, built on the site of the old Fencing School.
why: The roof opens in 40 seconds to reveal the sky — one of the most unusual theatre buildings in Europe.
tip: Tours run in the daytime; an evening show is a good rainy-Sunday alternative to the Philharmonic.

name: AmberSky Ferris Wheel
desc: A 50-metre wheel on Ołowianka with enclosed gondolas, three slow loops over the Motława and the shipyard cranes.
why: The only way to see the city from above without 400 stairs, and it is warm inside.
tip: Go at dusk for the lights. It stops in strong wind — not a Sunday option.

name: Polish Baltic Philharmonic
desc: A converted 19th-century power station on the water, now one of Poland's best halls.
why: Sunday 25 Oct, 19:00: Joanna Knitter & Baltic Banda play film music and pop standards — not stiff classical.
tip: Book online; dress smart-casual, jeans are fine.

name: Baltic Opera (Opera Bałtycka)
desc: Gdańsk's opera and ballet company, in a big socialist-modernist house near Wrzeszcz.
why: Only worth it if there is a title you actually like on your dates — check the repertoire.
tip: It is 15 min from your flat by tram; a taxi back at 22:30 is ~30 zł.

name: Teatr Wybrzeże
desc: The city's main drama stage, in a converted building on Targ Węglowy next to the U7 bowling.
why: Polish-language, so go for the atmosphere rather than the plot — or skip it.
tip: If you do not speak Polish, choose the Philharmonic instead.

name: Kino Neptun
desc: A small cinema in the middle of the Old Town showing mainstream films in original language with Polish subtitles.
why: A cheap, warm two-hour escape when the rain is horizontal.
tip: English-language films are usually subtitled, not dubbed — check before buying.

name: Gdańsk Shipyard walk
desc: Working post-industrial shipyard: 21 giant cranes, dry docks, red-brick halls and the Monument to the Fallen Shipyard Workers.
why: Where the 20th century turned, and it still smells of steel and sea. Free.
tip: Do it in daylight and finish on ul. Elektryków for a drink under the cranes.

name: Zaspa Murals
desc: A concrete housing estate covered in 60+ giant murals by international street artists — Europe's biggest open-air gallery of its kind.
why: Completely off the tourist trail, free, and photogenic.
tip: SKM from Gdańsk Główny to Gdańsk Zaspa, 6 min, 4.80 zł. Wear comfortable shoes — it is spread out.

name: Wyspa Spichrzów (Granary Island)
desc: The rebuilt granary island: brick warehouses turned into hotels and bars, with a new footbridge to the Old Town.
why: The best evening walk in Gdańsk — lights on the water, no traffic, bars along the quay.
tip: Cross the new pedestrian bridge from Długie Pobrzeże and walk the loop at blue hour.

name: Solidarity Square & Monument
desc: The square where the 1980 strikes were negotiated, with the towering monument of three crosses and anchors.
why: Thirty seconds from ECS and free — the emotional centre of the city's modern history.
tip: Read the inscriptions on the wall behind the crosses; they list the demands of the strikers.

name: Oliwa Park
desc: A French-style garden with clipped hedges, canals, a palm house and 300-year-old trees behind the cathedral.
why: Late-October colour, almost nobody on a Monday morning, and it is free.
tip: Enter from the cathedral side, walk the main alley, exit towards ul. Cystersów for the tram.

name: Gdańsk Zoo
desc: One of Poland's largest zoos, set in a forested valley with giraffes, elephants and a lot of uphill walking.
why: Cheap in October (30 vs 45 zł) and the autumn forest is beautiful.
tip: Hilly and big — only if you want a nature half-day. Entry closes 16:00 sharp.

name: Brzeźno Beach & Pier
desc: A 136-metre wooden pier over the Baltic, wide sand, pine trees and a promenade of fish shacks.
why: Sea, 20 minutes from the Old Town, free. Sunset with a beer from the nearby shop is the best ending to a dry day.
tip: Uber ~35 zł or tram ~25 min. Windy and cold — take the jacket.

name: Jelitkowo Beach
desc: A quieter, sandier beach between Brzeźno and Sopot, with a long promenade and pine woods behind it.
why: Where locals walk their dogs at sunset — same sea as Brzeźno with a fraction of the people.
tip: Walk from Brzeźno along the promenade (25 min) instead of doubling back.

name: Stogi Beach
desc: A wide, wild beach on the eastern side of the harbour, reachable by tram 9 from the centre.
why: The most local, least touristed beach in Gdańsk — but the tram ride is 35 minutes.
tip: Only worth it if you have a car or want a genuinely empty beach.

name: Sobieszewo Island & Ptasi Raj
desc: A sandy island between the Martwa Wisła and the sea, with the Ptasi Raj bird reserve, dunes and empty beaches.
why: The wildest nature within Gdańsk city limits, and you will see more birds than people.
tip: Needs a car or a long bus ride (1 h). Best in spring/autumn migration; bring binoculars.

name: Pachołek Hill (Sopot)
desc: The highest hill in the Tricity (109 m), with a viewing tower over the bay, forests and the sea.
why: A proper forest walk with a panorama — 25 minutes uphill from Sopot station, free.
tip: Wear shoes with grip; the last stretch is steep and muddy after rain.

name: Dolina Radości (Trójmiejski Park)
desc: A wooded valley in the Tricity Landscape Park with streams, beech forest and marked walking trails.
why: Real forest 15 minutes from the city — the best autumn walk if you want to leave the streets.
tip: Start at Oliwa and walk up; the trails are marked but muddy in October.

name: Sopot Beach
desc: A wide, soft-sand beach right in front of the pier, with beach bars and the Grand Hotel behind it.
why: The classic Tricity beach — and the pier is free after 30 September.
tip: Avoid Sunday morning: the Sopot Half Marathon closes the promenade and roads.

name: Orłowo Cliff (Gdynia)
desc: A 60-metre cliff of glacial till dropping into the sea, with a pier and a forest walk on top.
why: The most dramatic coastline in the Tricity — 30 min by SKM to Gdynia Orłowo.
tip: Do not stand under the cliff: it erodes and drops. Walk the top path instead.

name: Motława waterfront
desc: The river quay from the Green Gate to the Crane: barges, granaries, bridges and the best-lit evening walk.
why: Free, beautiful, and where every boat trip starts.
tip: Walk it at 17:15–17:45 for sunset plus city lights.

name: Góra Gradowa
desc: A grassy fort hill with a big cross, earthworks and a 360° view over the cranes and the Old Town roofs.
why: Free sunset spot 10 minutes from the centre, and nobody knows about it.
tip: Bring a beer and a jacket — it is exposed and windy.

name: Oruński Park
desc: A 19th-century landscape park in the south of the city with ponds, old trees and a stream.
why: A genuine local park, far from tourists — only if you are exploring beyond the centre.
tip: Not worth a special trip on a 3-day visit.

name: Mewia Łacha Reserve
desc: A sandbank reserve at the mouth of the Vistula where seals haul out and thousands of birds stop on migration.
why: The only place near Gdańsk where you might see a seal — but it is a full-day trip by car.
tip: Binoculars and a car needed; check the ferry across the Martwa Wisła.

name: Pierogarnia Mandu
desc: Gdańsk's famous pierogi: hand-folded, baked and boiled, from potato-cheese to duck and cherry.
why: The best pierogi in the city and the meal everyone remembers. Big portions, fair prices.
tip: Book online for 5 — walk-ins wait 30–60 min at dinner. Order two kinds each and share.

name: Bar mleczny Neptun
desc: A communist-era milk bar: trays, laminated menus, borscht, pierogi, breaded pork and compote.
why: A full hot meal for 25 zł in the middle of the tourist zone — the best value in Gdańsk.
tip: Order at the counter, pay at the till, collect at the hatch. Borscht + croquettes is the move.

name: Brovarnia
desc: A brewery-restaurant in a converted granary with copper tanks, river views and solid Polish cooking.
why: Big tables, own beer, and food that soaks up the evening — the safest 'everyone is happy' dinner.
tip: Book for 5 at 19:30 and ask for a window table. Pork knuckle to share.

name: Ryba Piła
desc: Baltic fish done simply — herring, cod, flounder, halibut — grilled or fried with good bread.
why: You are on the Baltic; eat the fish. Lighter than the pork-and-dumplings circuit.
tip: Ask what came in that morning. Fried cod + herring starter.

name: Tawerna Dominikańska
desc: A long-running waterfront tavern with fish, pierogi and a big terrace over the Motława.
why: Terrace on the water in summer, fireplace inside in October — good for a slow group lunch.
tip: Lunch menu is much cheaper than dinner; ask for it.

name: Restauracja Kubicki
desc: One of Gdańsk's oldest restaurants, serving duck, goose and old-Polish dishes in vaulted rooms.
why: If you want one proper sit-down Polish dinner with linen and a wine list, this is it.
tip: Book ahead; mains 60–90 zł. The duck with apples is the signature.

name: Piwnica Rajców
desc: A 14th-century cellar under Artus Court turned beer hall, with own-brewed beer and hearty plates.
why: Vaulted brick cellars, long tables, beer brewed on site — the most atmospheric group dinner in the centre.
tip: Ask for the tasting board of four beers; it is cheaper than four pints.

name: Karczma Piwna 'Gdański Bowke'
desc: Rustic Polish tavern on the waterfront: bigos, żurek, ribs, and portions built for hungry people.
why: Unpretentious, filling and right on the river — good when everyone is too hungry to choose.
tip: Order the żurek in bread and one plate of ribs to share.

name: Zafishowani
desc: Serious seafood: oysters, turbot, Baltic fish, a long wine list and a chef who knows what he is doing.
why: The one 'nice' dinner of the trip if you want to spend properly.
tip: Reserve 2 days ahead and say it is a group of five; the tasting menu needs notice.

name: Gambas Seafood & Meat
desc: Spanish-leaning seafood and dry-aged steaks in a brick cellar off Długa.
why: Good middle ground when half the table wants fish and half wants meat.
tip: The mixed grill for two is enormous — order one for three people.

name: Bistro Pobite Gary
desc: A neighbourhood bistro doing modern Polish plates with seasonal ingredients, near the Politechnika.
why: Ten minutes from your flat, no tourists, and the best value cooking on this list.
tip: Lunch set (12:00–16:00) is ~30 zł for two courses.

name: Zielona Papuga
desc: A long-standing vegetarian restaurant in a leafy Wrzeszcz villa, with a garden in summer.
why: If one of you does not eat meat, this is where nobody compromises.
tip: Book the garden table if the weather holds; the beetroot tartare converts people.

name: Restauracja Pueblo
desc: Tacos, quesadillas and margaritas in a colourful room off Długa.
why: A reliable change of pace from pierogi, and the margaritas are strong.
tip: Taco sharing platters are the cheapest way to feed five.

name: Hola Tapas
desc: A tiny Spanish tapas bar on Piwna: jamón, tortilla, patatas bravas, vermouth on tap.
why: Perfect for a pre-crawl snack and a vermouth — stand at the bar like locals.
tip: Order 6–8 plates for five and share; the tortilla sells out early.

name: Chinkalnia
desc: Georgian food — khinkali dumplings, khachapuri cheese bread, walnut salads — in a warm room.
why: The best-value 'new' cuisine in Gdańsk and ideal for sharing after a cold walk.
tip: Order one khachapuri for the table and 3 khinkali each; do not order more, it is heavy.

name: Gyozilla
desc: Gyoza, bao and ramen in a small modern spot near the Politechnika.
why: Fast, cheap, close to your flat, and open when everything else has a queue.
tip: The pan-fried gyoza set is the order; 12 pieces for ~30 zł.

name: Pyra Bar
desc: Everything potato: baked potatoes with toppings, pyzy, potato pancakes — cheap and filling.
why: The cheapest sit-down meal near Długi Targ after the milk bar, and genuinely good.
tip: One baked potato with two toppings is enough per person.

name: Bar Przystań
desc: A fish shack by the Brzeźno pier: fried cod, herring, chips, eaten at picnic tables facing the sea.
why: The best possible ending to a beach walk — fried fish with the Baltic in front of you.
tip: Cash is handy; the queue moves fast. Check it is open in late October.

name: Bar-Rybakówka
desc: A scruffy, beloved fish bar near Stągiewna: herring, cod, fish soup, plastic trays.
why: Cheap, fast, local, and 3 minutes from the river — the anti-tourist lunch.
tip: Order the fish soup and the fried herring; sit upstairs by the window.

name: Mnie to Rybka
desc: A modern fish restaurant with Baltic catch, oysters and a short seasonal menu.
why: Better than the waterfront taverns at similar prices, and less crowded.
tip: Ask for the catch of the day, not the menu classics.

name: Kos
desc: A big, busy all-day restaurant on Piwna with pizza, salads, burgers and a long drinks list.
why: Handles groups without booking, which is rare in the Old Town on a Saturday.
tip: Go before 19:00 or expect 20 minutes at the bar.

name: Canis
desc: Proper Italian: pasta made in-house, wood-fired pizza, decent wine by the glass.
why: The best Italian in the centre and a safe bet for five fussy eaters.
tip: The cacio e pepe and the diavola are the two orders.

name: Mono
desc: A small modern kitchen doing seasonal Polish plates with a tasting-menu mentality.
why: If you want one 'foodie' dinner without the Zafishowani price, this is it.
tip: Book; the menu changes weekly and the tasting option is the value.

name: Manna 68
desc: A vegetarian institution on Świętego Ducha with a daily buffet and a la carte.
why: Cheap, healthy and open all day — good for the morning after.
tip: The buffet is priced by weight; load up on the salads.

name: Avocado
desc: A vegan bistro on Wajdeloty with bowls, burgers and very good cakes.
why: Wajdeloty street is where young Gdańsk eats — this is its anchor.
tip: Try the seitan burger; the cakes are the real reason to come.

name: Pomelo
desc: A bright bistro doing Polish classics with a lighter, modern hand.
why: Good middle-price dinner near the river without the karczma heaviness.
tip: The duck pierogi and the seasonal soup are the picks.

name: Swojski Smak
desc: A canteen-style Polish restaurant with home cooking: schabowy, pierogi, soups, compote.
why: Where office workers eat — cheap, fast, and the portions are enormous.
tip: Lunch before 15:00 is the cheapest; the schabowy is plate-sized.

name: Hacjenda
desc: A wooden hunting-lodge-style restaurant in Oliwa with game, dumplings and a big garden.
why: Good lunch stop after the Oliwa cathedral and park — 10 minutes' walk.
tip: The wild boar stew and the potato pancakes are the signatures.

name: Fellini
desc: A long-running Italian with pizza, pasta and a garden courtyard off Długa.
why: Reliable, central, and good for a quick carb-load before a night out.
tip: Pizza is better than the pasta here.

name: San Marco
desc: An old-school Italian trattoria with white tablecloths and a big wine list.
why: The 'proper dinner' Italian — quieter than the pizza places.
tip: Book a table; the seafood risotto is the dish.

name: Trattoria La Cantina
desc: A family-run trattoria with fresh pasta and a garden behind the Old Town.
why: Cheap-ish, generous and friendly — a good group fallback.
tip: Ask for the daily pasta, not the menu.

name: Faro Gdańsk
desc: Wood-fired pizza with Polish ingredients in a big, loud room.
why: Good for a fast, cheap dinner when the group cannot agree.
tip: Two pizzas for three people is enough.

name: Burgermania
desc: Big, messy burgers and fries near the station.
why: The best burger near Gdańsk Główny — useful before or after a train.
tip: The double bacon is the order; the queue is fast.

name: Grulle
desc: Polish street food done well: zapiekanki, kiełbasa, potato pancakes, oscypek.
why: Cheap, fast and very Polish — good late-night food after the bars.
tip: Open late; the oscypek with cranberry is the best 15 zł you will spend.

name: Restauracja Republika
desc: A casual pizza-and-pasta place with a big terrace on the river.
why: Cheap, central and always open — the safe option when plans collapse.
tip: Terrace is the reason; the pizza is fine, not special.

name: Motlava
desc: A modern Polish restaurant in the new shipyard development, with a view of the cranes.
why: Good dinner before or after ECS, in the most interesting new part of the city.
tip: Ask for a window table facing the cranes.

name: Neighbour's Kitchen
desc: A small kitchen on Szafarnia doing seasonal Polish plates and a good lunch set.
why: Better value than the waterfront places 50 m away, and quieter.
tip: Lunch set is ~35 zł; go before 15:00.

name: Eliksir
desc: A stylish modern restaurant in a converted villa near the Politechnika.
why: Close to your flat, good cocktails, and a menu that suits a group.
tip: Book; the bar is worth staying at after dinner.

name: Wozownia Gdańska
desc: A restored carriage house in Oliwa serving Polish game and fish.
why: The nicest lunch near the Oliwa cathedral, in a beautiful room.
tip: The venison and the beetroot soup are the reasons to come.

name: Rękawiczka
desc: A quirky bistro with a changing international menu and a cosy room.
why: Good if you want something other than Polish food without going to a chain.
tip: Check the daily board; it is better than the printed menu.

name: Panorama
desc: A restaurant on the 6th floor with a panorama over the shipyard and the Old Town.
why: The view is the point — go at sunset for a drink even if you eat elsewhere.
tip: Book a window table and go 30 min before sunset.

name: Targ Rybny Fishmarkt
desc: A fish market and bistro on the waterfront: pick your fish, they cook it.
why: Fresh fish without the restaurant markup, eaten at a shared table.
tip: Go before 17:00 when the counter is fullest.

name: Sushi Siedem
desc: A reliable sushi chain with big sets and a view over Długie Pobrzeże.
why: If someone in the group does not eat Polish food, this solves it.
tip: Order the big set for 4 and add one roll.

name: Bar A-Dong
desc: A cheap, fast Vietnamese/Asian canteen: pho, noodles, spring rolls.
why: The best cheap eat in the centre after the milk bars.
tip: Pho is 25 zł and better than places charging twice.

name: Unicorn
desc: Falafel, hummus, shakshuka and grilled meats near the hipodrom.
why: Cheap, vegetarian-friendly and open late — good after a night out.
tip: The mixed grill plate feeds two; the hummus is excellent.

name: Faloviec
desc: A plant-based canteen in a Falowiec block — Polish food without the meat.
why: A weird, wonderful location inside Europe's longest housing block.
tip: The 'schabowy' made of seitan is the joke and the order.

name: Zagroda Rybacka
desc: A fish farm and restaurant on Sobieszewo Island, serving what they smoke themselves.
why: Only if you have a car and want a proper out-of-town lunch by the water.
tip: The smoked eel and the fish soup are the point.

name: Drukarnia Cafe
desc: A big café in a former printing house right on the Motława, with sofas and a long window.
why: The best place to sit with a coffee and watch the river when it rains.
tip: Upstairs window seats are the ones to take.

name: Kawiarnia Retro
desc: A tiny old-school café on Piwna with mismatched furniture and cheap coffee.
why: Authentic, cheap, and the kind of place that has not changed in 20 years.
tip: Cash preferred; the cheesecake is homemade.

name: Fika
desc: A Scandinavian-style café on Szeroka with proper filter coffee, cinnamon buns and brunch plates.
why: The best coffee in the Old Town and a good sit-down breakfast.
tip: Weekend brunch fills up — go before 11:00.

name: Kawana
desc: A specialty coffee bar on Wallenroda with single-origin beans and a quiet room.
why: If you care about coffee, this is the best in the city.
tip: Ask what is on filter; they will talk you through it.

name: Cukiernia Sowa
desc: A Polish patisserie chain that does excellent cakes, cheesecake and coffee.
why: Cheap, reliable sugar stop near the station and in the centre.
tip: The szarlotka (apple cake) is the order.

name: Pankejk
desc: American-style pancakes, thick and stacked, with sweet and savoury toppings.
why: The hangover cure on Długa — big portions, open all day.
tip: The bacon-and-maple stack is the move; share one if you had a big night.

name: Latto Gelato
desc: Small-batch gelato with rotating flavours, made on site.
why: The best ice cream in the centre, even in October.
tip: Try the salted caramel and the plum.

name: Mamma Mia il Gelato
desc: A gelateria on the Oliwa route with proper Italian-style ice cream.
why: The natural stop after the cathedral and park.
tip: Pistachio is the test — it passes.

name: Kotka Cafe
desc: A cat café in a villa in Oliwa — coffee, cake and a lot of resident cats.
why: Only if someone in the group actually likes cats; otherwise skip.
tip: Book a slot; they limit entry.

name: Pożegnanie z Afryką
desc: A Polish coffee roaster and café on Świętojańska, roasting since the 1990s.
why: Buy beans here as a souvenir — better than anything at the airport.
tip: Ask for the freshly roasted single origin.

name: Corten Café
desc: A café inside the ECS building with industrial concrete and a view of the shipyard.
why: Warm, quiet, and you can sit without buying a museum ticket.
tip: Enter through the main ECS lobby.

name: Fukafe
desc: A neighbourhood café on Wajdeloty street with excellent cakes and a young crowd.
why: Wajdeloty is the best street for cafés in Gdańsk — this is the anchor.
tip: Sit outside if it is dry; the street is pedestrian.
